title: A utility piezoelectric energy harvester with low frequency and high-output voltage: Theoretical model, experimental verification and energy storage

sections.heading: A utility piezoelectric energy harvester with low frequency and high-output voltage: Theoretical model, experimental verification and energy storage
sections.text: Guangyi Zhang, Shiqiao Gao, and Haipeng Liu

sections.heading: A utility piezoelectric energy harvester with low frequency and high-output voltage: Theoretical model, experimental verification and energy storage
sections.text:
Guangyi Zhang,a Shiqiao Gao, and Haipeng Liu   
State Key Laboratory of Explosion Science and Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology,   
Beijing, 100081, China

(Received 22 June 2016; accepted 6 September 2016; published online 13 September 2016)

In this paper, a utility piezoelectric energy harvester with low frequency and highoutput voltage is presented. Firstly, the harvester’s three theoretical models are presented, namely the static model, the quasi static model and the dynamic vibration model. By analyzing the influence of the mass ratio of the mass block to the beam on output characteristics of the harvester, we compare the quasi static model and the dynamic vibration model and then define their applicable ranges. Secondly, simulation and experiments are done to verify the models, using the harvester with PZT-5H piezoelectric material, which are proved to be consistent with each other. The experimental results show that the output open-circuit voltage and the output power can reach up to $8 6 . 3 6 \mathrm { V }$ and $2 7 . 5 \mathrm { m W }$ respectively. The experiments are conducted when this harvester system is excited by the first modal frequency $( 5 8 . 9 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ with the acceleration $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . In this low frequency vibration case, it is easy to capture the energy in the daily environment. In addition, LTC 3588-1 chip (Linear Technology Corporation) is used as the medium energy circuit to transfer charges from the PZT-5H electrode to the 0.22F 5V super capacitor and ML621 rechargeable button battery. For this super-capacitor, it takes about $1 0 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ for the capacitor voltage to rise from 0V to 3.6V. For this button battery, it takes about $2 0 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ to increase the battery voltage from $2 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ to 3.48V. $©$ 2016 Author(s). sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
In recent years, wireless intelligent sensor network1 and wearable electronic devices2 have been developed rapidly in the fields of military affairs, medical science, energy, roads and bridges. However, the energy supply of these devices has always been a key problem. As the main energy, chemical batteries have some disadvantages, such as short storage time, large volume, and inability to integrate with MEMS devices. In addition, for some sensors, their installation positions are not suitable for replacing the chemical batteries. Therefore, as an energy substitute for chemical batteries, the piezoelectric energy harvester that can obtain energy from the vibration environment becomes a hot research topic.3–5 The piezoelectric energy harvester has many advantages, such as simple structure, easy miniaturization, no fever, no electromagnetic interference and no pollution, meeting the energy demand of low power consumption products. Thus, it is becoming an important choice of energy harvesting devices.

There are many factors influencing the performance of piezoelectric energy harvesters, like resonance frequency, resonance voltage and structure type, etc. For resonance frequency, most of the vibrating energy harvesters work at the frequency of more than $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ,3,4,6,7 making them well suited for harvesting energy from rotating machinery. However, in daily life, the vibration frequencies of various vibration sources are mainly in the range of $1 { \sim } 1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . For example, the vibration frequency of a vehicle is concentrated in the range of $0 . 5 { \sim } 5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ; the ground vibration frequency of a train is about $5 { \sim } 8 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ;8 and the vibration frequency of human motion is typically in the range of $1 { \sim } 3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Therefore, there is great significance of researching low frequency piezoelectric energy harvesters.

In the aspect of the structure, due to obtaining deformation response easily, the piezoelectric energy harvester with a flexible cantilever beam becomes one of the main structural forms. For this structure, a lot of related researches have been made, whether in the macro-structure $( \mathrm { m m } \mathrm { s i z e } ) ^ { 9 - 1 1 }$ or in the MEMS structure (micron size).12,13 There are two main problems for existing structures, one is the high frequency resonance frequency, which is difficult to harvest energy in the daily environment. The other one is that the output voltage and power is low, making it difficult to be stored and used by the circuit rectifier.

In the theoretical analysis of structural vibration, the vibration system model is established by simplifying the cantilever beam (including mass) system into a spring-mass system of SDOF.14,15 It is convenient to analyze system response and mechano-electric coupling characteristics of piezoelectric materials. From the point of view of system vibration, the simplification seems to solve the problem of vibration response. However, from the perspective of piezoelectric effects, many important effect factors are lost. In order to avoid analysis errors caused by simplification, Sodano et al. (2004, 2005) and DuToit et al. (2007), according to the Euler-Bernoulli beam hypothesis, synthetically use Hamilton variational principle and Rayleigh-Ritz method to analyze the vibration system, but this way is more suitable for numerical calculation instead of analytical solutions. In addition, there are also some studies between the two ways mentioned above, such as one-modal analysis16 and constant curvature analysis,17 etc. These studies have also made some assumptions, which affect the analysis of the electromechanical coupling effects. Therefore, based on the hypothesis of Euler-Bernoulli beam, Erturk et al. (2008)18,19 gave an analysis model of distribution load and quality. In this model, external excitation can be arbitrary functions, and the correction factor is introduced to improve the existing method (single degree of freedom), but it neglects the influence of the mass block on the natural frequency and vibration mode of the vibration system.

About theoretical verification, Muthalif et al. $( 2 0 1 \dot { 5 } ) ^ { 2 0 }$ made a dynamic theoretical model with a cantilever beam structure, but the theoretical model has not been compared with the test results in the paper. Then, the dynamic vibration model7 is deduced and verified by the test, but the working frequency of the structure they made is relatively high $( 1 8 5 \mathrm { H z } { \sim } 2 1 5 \mathrm { H z } )$ , which is very difficult to capture power from the low frequency vibration environment with high energy density.

In this paper, a utility piezoelectric energy harvester with low frequency and high-output voltage is presented. Firstly, according to Euler-Bernoulli beam hypothesis the harvester’s three theoretical models are presented systematically, namely the static model, the quasi static model and the dynamic vibration model, which are clear and concise in showing the relationship between the structure parameters and the results. And by analyzing the influence of the mass ratio of the mass block to the beam on output characteristics of the harvester, we compare the quasi static model with the dynamic vibration model and define their applicable ranges. Then, we use the piezoelectric energy harvester with PZT-5H piezoelectric material to do simulation and experiments and find that the theoretical results are in good agreement with the simulation results and experimental ones. The results of experiments show that the first modal frequency of the structure is $5 8 . 9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ (corresponding theoretical value is $5 9 . 7 2 \mathrm { H z } $ ). The first modal open-circuit voltage can reach 86.3v (corresponding theoretical value is 93.5v). In addition, the circuit of energy acquisition is configured with LTC3588-1 chip to charge the super-capacitor and the rechargeable battery. This paper is organized as follows: Sec. II describes the theoretical study on the static model, the quasi static model and the dynamic vibration model. In Sec. III, the theoretical models are verified by simulation analysis and verification experiments. And in Sec. IV, the energy acquisition circuit is configured with LTC3588-1 chip and the charging test of the super-capacitor and the rechargeable button battery is also made. Conclusions are given in Sec. V.

sections.heading: II. THEORETICAL STUDY ON THE UTILITY PIEZOELECTRIC ENERGY HARVESTER
sections.text: The utility piezoelectric energy harvester comprises an elastic cantilever beam, a mass block and a PZT-5H piezoelectric plate polarized along the vertical direction. The elastic cantilever beam and the mass block are made of stainless steel, being used to adjust the resonant frequency and the amplitude of the output voltage of the harvester. The PZT-5H piezoelectric plate is covered with a layer of silver electrode on its upper and lower surfaces. The silver electrode is used as the cathode and the anode to output energy. The structural model diagram is shown in Fig. 1.

sections.heading: A. Static vibration model
sections.text:
Since the deformation of the beam is small and in the linear range, the cantilever beam with the PZT-5H piezoelectric plate can be assumed to be Euler-Bernoulli beam.18,19,21,22 Because of the PZT-5H piezoelectric plate, the neutral plane is not coincident with the geometrical center of the cantilever beam. The actual neutral plane is the plane where both tensile stress and compressive stress are zero when the beam generates bending deformation. The stress of the piezoelectric material and the elastic cantilever beam can be expressed as23

$$
\begin{array} { r } { T _ { p } = Y _ { p } \displaystyle \frac { z } { \rho } } \\ { T _ { s } = Y _ { s } \displaystyle \frac { z } { \rho } } \end{array}
$$

where $Y _ { p }$ and $Y _ { s }$ are young’s modulus of the piezoelectric material and the base beam, respectively. $\rho$ is curvature radius of the beam’s neutral plane, and $z$ is the coordinate for the direction of thickness starting from neutral plane. Without considering the inverse piezoelectric effect, the relationship of total stress in the cross section can be expressed as

$$
\int _ { A } { T _ { 1 } d A } = \int _ { e } ^ { e + \delta } T _ { p } b d z + \int _ { - ( h - e ) } ^ { e } T _ { s } b d z = 0
$$

where $T _ { 1 }$ is the total stress, $A$ is the neutral plane, $e$ is the distance between the neutral plane and the interface of the piezoelectric material and the base beam, $h$ is the thickness of the base beam, $\delta$ is the thickness of the material, $^ b$ δis the width of the beam. The cross sectional view of a unimorph cantilever beam is shown in Fig. 2.

Employing Eqs. (1) and (2) into Eq. (3), one may obtain

$$
e = \frac { Y _ { s } h ^ { 2 } - Y _ { p } \delta ^ { 2 } } { 2 ( Y _ { p } \delta + Y _ { s } h ) }
$$

It can be seen that the position of the neutral surface is determined by the material and the structure size of the beam. The curvature radius of the neutral surface depends on the bending degree of the beam, which is determined by the bending moment of the external force and the stiffness of the composite beam (the cantilever beam with the PZT-5H piezoelectric plate). According to the moment balance condition, when we do not considering the influence of the inverse piezoelectric effect and the external electric field, the moment of any cross section can be expressed as18,19,22

$$
M = \int _ { A } T _ { 1 } z d A = \int _ { - ( h - e ) } ^ { e } b Y _ { s } { \frac { z } { \rho } } z d z + \int _ { e } ^ { e + \delta } b Y _ { p } { \frac { z } { \rho } } z d z
$$

The bending equation of the general beam is expressed as24

$$
Y I { \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } w } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } } = M
$$

where $w$ is the deformation deflection (neutral surface), $Y I$ is the bending stiffness of the composite beam, $Y$ is the equivalent elastic modulus, $I$ is the equivalent inertia moment of the cross section. The bending stiffness of the composite beam can be written as19

$$
Y I = \frac { b [ Y _ { s } ( h ^ { 3 } - 3 h ^ { 2 } e + 3 h e ^ { 2 } ) + Y _ { p } ( \delta ^ { 3 } + 3 \delta ^ { 2 } e + 3 \delta e ^ { 2 } ) ] } { 3 }
$$

From another point of view, when the cantilever beam structure is affected by the external force or the structure vibrates at a very low speed, the inertia of the beam and the mass can be ignored. Thus, the cantilever beam structure can be analyzed with the method of static bending. The static equilibrium relationship is shown in Fig. 3.

Based on the static equilibrium relationship, the bending moment of the section $\textrm { C }$ (arbitrary coordinate) is:

$$
M = m _ { 2 } a ( L - x ) + \int _ { 0 } ^ { L - x } s q d s = m _ { 2 } a ( L - x ) + { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \frac { m _ { 1 } a } { L } } ( L - x ) ^ { 2 }
$$

where $m _ { 1 }$ is the mass of the base beam, $m _ { 2 }$ is the mass of the mass block, $L$ is the length of the beam, $a$ is the inertia acceleration, $q$ is the line density of the beam (mass per unit length).

Solving Eq. (5) and employing the curvature radius into Eq. (3), one may obtain

$$
T _ { p } = Y _ { p } \frac { z } { \rho } = \frac { 3 Y _ { p } [ m _ { 2 } a ( L - x ) + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \frac { m _ { 1 } a } { L } ( L - x ) ^ { 2 } ] z } { b [ Y _ { s } ( h ^ { 3 } - 3 h ^ { 2 } e + 3 h e ^ { 2 } ) + Y _ { p } ( \delta ^ { 3 } + 3 \delta ^ { 2 } e + 3 \delta e ^ { 2 } ) ] }
$$

In order to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy, the following piezoelectric coupling constitutive equation is used:25

$$
D _ { 3 } = d _ { 3 1 } T _ { p } + \varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { \mathrm { T } } E _ { 3 }
$$

where $D _ { 3 }$ is the electric displacement, $d _ { 3 1 }$ is piezoelectric constant, $T _ { p }$ is stress, $\varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is permittivity at constant stress, $E _ { 3 }$ εis uniform electric field. When the applied electric field is zero, the charge density

$$
Q _ { t o p } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { L } b D _ { 3 } ( x , e + \delta ) d x = \frac { d _ { 3 1 } Y _ { p } [ 3 m _ { 2 } + m _ { 1 } ] a L ^ { 2 } ( e + \delta ) } { 2 [ Y _ { s } ( h ^ { 3 } - 3 h ^ { 2 } e + 3 h e ^ { 2 } ) + Y _ { p } ( \delta ^ { 3 } + 3 \delta ^ { 2 } e + 3 \delta e ^ { 2 } ) ] }

$$

Similarly, the charge density of the lower electrode can be expressed as

$$
\sigma _ { l o w } = - D _ { 3 } ( x , e ) = - \frac { 3 d _ { 3 1 } Y _ { p } [ m _ { 2 } a ( L - x ) + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \frac { m _ { 1 } a } { L } ( L - x ) ^ { 2 } ] e } { b [ Y _ { s } ( h ^ { 3 } - 3 h ^ { 2 } e + 3 h e ^ { 2 } ) + Y _ { p } ( \delta ^ { 3 } + 3 \delta ^ { 2 } e + 3 \delta e ^ { 2 } ) ] }

The total charge quantity of the lower electrode can be expressed as

$$

$$

It can be seen that the charge of the upper and lower electrodes are not the same, which shows that the electric field in the medium is not uniform. For an inhomogeneous electric field, the voltage between the two poles is:

$$
V ( x ) = \int _ { e } ^ { e + \delta } E _ { 3 } ( x , z ) d z = E _ { 0 } \frac { 1 } { \bar { \rho } } ( e + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \delta ) \delta
$$

where $E _ { 0 }$ is the equivalent electric field intensity, and can be deduced as

$$
E _ { 0 } = \frac { d _ { 3 1 } Y _ { p } } { \varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { \mathrm { S } } }
$$

where $\varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ is the permittivity without stress.

sections.heading: B. Quasi static vibration model (SDOF)
sections.text:
Considering the inertia of the mass block and neglecting the inertia of the elastic cantilever beam, the dynamic equation of the mechanical system is expressed as18,19,26

$$
m _ { 2 } \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } w } { \partial t ^ { 2 } } | _ { x = L }  + c \frac { \partial w } { \partial t } + k w | _ { x = L } = f | _ { x = L } 
$$

where $c$ is damping coefficient, $f$ is inertia force, $k$ is the equivalent stiffness of the cantilever beam. The equivalent stiffness can be written as

$$
k = \frac { 2 Y I } { L ^ { 3 } }
$$

The natural frequency of the system is deduced as

$$
\omega = \sqrt { \frac { k } { m _ { 2 } } } = \sqrt { \frac { 2 Y I } { m _ { 2 } L ^ { 3 } } } = \sqrt { 2 } \sqrt { \frac { Y I } { m _ { 2 } L ^ { 3 } } }
$$

When the excitation frequency is as same as the natural frequency, external excitation can be expressed as

$$
f = m _ { 2 } a ( t ) = m _ { 2 } A \sin \omega t
$$

where $A$ is the acceleration amplitude of the excited vibration, the amplitude of the resonant response of the system is deduced as

$$
\bar { w } = \frac { A } { 2 \zeta \omega ^ { 2 } }
$$

$\begin{array} { r } { \zeta = \frac { c } { 2 \omega m _ { 2 } } } \end{array}$

ζ ω In addition, through the mechanical analysis of the beam structure, the bending curvature of the elastic cantilever beam is expressed as

$$
{ \cfrac { 1 } { \rho } } = { \cfrac { \partial ^ { 2 } w } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } } = { \cfrac { L f } { Y I } }
$$

The rotation angle of the end of the beam is expressed as

$$
\theta = \frac { \partial w } { \partial x } \mid _ { x = L } = \frac { L ^ { 2 } f } { Y I }
$$

For this case that the piezoelectric plate is covered with electrodes, the charge quantity and the voltage are respectively expressed as

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle Q _ { t o p } = b d _ { 3 1 } Y _ { p } ( e + \delta ) \frac { L ^ { 2 } f } { Y I } } } \\ { { \displaystyle Q _ { l o w } = - b d _ { 3 1 } Y _ { p } e \frac { L ^ { 2 } f } { Y I } } } \\ { { \displaystyle V ( x ) = E _ { 0 } \frac { L f } { Y I } ( e + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \delta ) \delta } } \end{array}
$$

However, because the piezoelectric material is a non-conductor, the inner polarization charge belongs to the bound charge. We need cover the whole upper and lower surfaces of the piezoelectric plate with silver electrodes to get the bound charges out. sections.heading: D. Model analysis and comparison
sections.text:
The applicable ranges of the static model, the quasi-static model and the dynamic model are different. The static model neglects the inertia of the beam and the mass block, assuming that the beam and the mass block acquire the same acceleration from external vibration. It is usually used in static environment. The quasi static model considers the inertia of the mass block, but neglects the inertia of the beam, so it can be applied in the structure with big mass ratio $\left( \mathrm { m } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { m } _ { 1 } \right)$ of the mass block to the beam or it can be used to estimate output performance of the harvester under low speed vibration. However, the dynamic model considers the inertia of both the mass block and the beam, suitable for dynamic environment, which is more accurate and more widely used than the previous two models.

To compare the quasi-static model and the dynamic model, we analyze the effect of changing mass ratio on the accuracy of them. The specific parameters of the structure are shown in Table I except the mass block. The results in Fig. 4 show that, with the mass ratio increasing, the gap between the two models becomes larger. However, in fact, voltage error is gradually reduced. For this cantilever beam structure, when the mass ratio reaches 13, the error of the first modal frequency between the two models will be less than $3 \%$ , and the error of the first modal displacement will be less than $10 \%$ .

![](images/43d495f29757de6260fcc901d5b59b8e08d653055e7a9689cd0725670a83ea1d.jpg)  
FIG. 4. The effect of mass ratio on the first modal voltage of the quasi static model and the dynamic model.

Under this circumstance, the dynamic model can be replaced by the quasi-static model to calculate and analyze because the quasi-static model is more concise.

sections.heading: III. SIMULATIONS AND EXPERIMENTAL VERIFICATION
sections.text:
In order to verify the theoretical model, we designed the corresponding structure model, as shown in Fig. 5.

The specific parameters of the structure size and the material used in the simulation model and the experiment prototype are shown in the Table I.

sections.heading: A. Simulation analysis
sections.text: According to the specific structure of the piezoelectric energy harvester, the model is simulated with COMSOL Multiphysics software. The simulation grid and the first order mode shape are shown in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7, respectively. Through simulation, when the acceleration is $1 0 \mathrm { m / s }$ , the first modal frequency of the structure is $5 9 . 6 3 \mathrm { H z }$ , the resonant peak voltage is $9 8 . 2 0 \mathrm { v }$ , as shown in Fig. 8.

sections.heading: B. Experiment analysis
sections.text:
In order to further verify the theoretical analysis and the simulation results, we designed the physical structure of single crystal piezoelectric energy harvester. And the related experimental studies were carried out. The structure prototype and the experiment setup are shown in Fig. 9 and Fig. 10.

Firstly, the natural frequency of the piezoelectric structure is obtained by frequency sweeping test and the first modal frequency is $5 8 . 9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Then, under the condition of constant acceleration, the open circuit voltage is tested when frequency is changing near the first modal frequency. When the acceleration is $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ , the open circuit voltage versus frequency variation is shown in Fig. 11. From the graph, the peak voltage is $8 6 . 3 6 \mathrm { v }$ at the first modal frequency.From the Fig. 12, there is a linear relationship between acceleration and the open-circuit voltage. In other words, when the frequency is constant, the open-circuit voltage increases linearly with increasing acceleration, which is consistent with the results of the theoretical model. In addition, the effects of load on the output voltage and the output power are shown in Fig. 13 and Fig. 14, respectively. From these two graphs, we can find that, the optimal load is about $3 3 . 9 \mathrm { K } \Omega$ and the maximum output power is up to $2 7 . 5 \mathrm { m W }$ .

sections.heading: IV. ENERGY STORAGE
sections.text:
The output current of the piezoelectric energy harvester is alternating current. However, micro and low power devices basically use DC power supply; and the short-time output energy of the harvester is too low to directly drive microelectronic devices. Therefore, an effective method for this predicament is to use rectifier circuit and storage devices as an intermediate link, which converts alternating current into direct current, accumulates and stores the energy, then supplies power to microelectronic devices. The flow chart of energy acquisition and storage is shown in Fig. 16.

![](images/0646677ea968e66981a371dda3ae6bca81fb5160d5e24f8b0ebfac02292df44c.jpg)  
FIG. 16. The flow chart of energy acquisition and storage.

![](images/bbeaa8c604e65c6b8962a79a5c3681ff5961ab4e4cf98bfb4e68e4c4c890d318.jpg)  
FIG. 17. The energy acquisition circuit diagram configured in the piezoelectric energy harvester.

In order to gain the electric energy from the piezoelectric energy harvester, an energy acquisition circuit is configured with LTC3588-1 chip, which has the function of rectifier and voltage regulator. The connection between the chip and the corresponding electronic components is shown in Fig. 17. In this figure, the piezoelectric energy harvester is connected to PZ1 and PZ2 on the circuit board. The energy acquisition circuit board with LTC3588-1 chip is connected to the output end of the harvester, which can be used to charge the super-capacitor and rechargeable battery.

![](images/c3775e477f3374db99ca0b66bb977452087705138f572df17d069d7c0cdd4f13.jpg)

The charging circuit and the super-capacitor/rechargeable battery are shown in Fig. 18. The experiment data from the charging process of the super-capacitor is recorded by a signal analyzer, as shown in Fig. 19. For this 0.22F 5V super-capacitor, it takes about $1 0 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ for its voltage to rise from 0V to $3 . 6 \mathrm { V }$ when the harvester is excited by the first modal with the experimental acceleration $1 . 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } 2$ . And for the ML621 rechargeable button battery (capacity: $5 . 8 \mathrm { m A h }$ ), it takes about $2 0 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ to increase the battery voltage from $2 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ to 3.48V, as shown in Fig. 20.

sections.heading: V. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
This paper synthetically presents the static, the quasi static and the dynamic mathematical models of the piezoelectric energy harvester with a cantilever beam. Simulation and experiments are done to verify the models, in which PZT-5H is used as piezoelectric material, stainless steel as the material of the base beam and the mass block. The results are consistent with the theoretical models, which can clearly see the relationship between the parameters and the results.

About the applicable ranges, the static model is usually used in static environment. The quasi static model can be applied in the structure with larger mass ratio of the mass block to the beam or it can be used to estimate the output performance of the harvester under low speed vibration. Compared with the former two models, the dynamic model is more widely used dynamic environment because it is more accurate.

In addition, the utility piezoelectric energy harvester structure can obtain very high voltage under the condition of low frequency vibration. This structure’s first modal frequency is $5 8 . 9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . When the acceleration is $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ , the output voltage is up to $8 6 . 3 6 \mathrm { V } ,$ and the maximum output power is up to $2 7 . 5 \mathrm { m W } .$ To gain and store the electric energy, the energy acquisition circuit is configured with LTC3588-1 chip. It takes about $1 0 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ for the 0.22F 5V super-capacitor to raise the voltage from 0V to 3.6V. And it takes about $2 0 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ for the ML621 rechargeable button battery (capacity: $5 . 8 \mathrm { m A h }$ ) to raise the battery voltage from 2.5V to 3.48V.
